key_insight: LLM judges can predict human preferences but they systematically weigh evaluation criteria differently than developers; TRACE automatically uncovers these rubric-level biases in realistic, partial-context code interactions.
problem_solved: Addresses the gap in evaluating LLMs as code judges under realistic interactive conditions (partial context and ambiguous intent) and identifies systematic differences between how humans and LLMs prioritize rubric items.
method: Introduce TRACE: a framework that tests LLM judges' ability to predict human preferences in interactive code tasks.
Automatically extract rubric items from judgment data to quantify how humans and models weight each criterion.
Empirically evaluate across three coding modalities (chat-based programming, IDE autocompletion, and a third coding interaction modality) to reveal consistent bias patterns.
impact: Helps practitioners understand and correct systematic biases in automated code evaluation, improving reliability and alignment of LLM-based reviewers in real-world developer workflows.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram of TRACE: input (partial context + ambiguous intent) → LLM judge → rubric extraction → human preference prediction
Side-by-side bar charts comparing weight/importance of top rubric items for developers vs. LLMs across modalities
Heatmap showing where LLMs' predictions diverge from human preferences (by rubric item and modality)
Example interaction UI mockup illustrating partial context and ambiguous intent scenarios used for evaluation
paper_title: Comparing Developer and LLM Biases in Code Evaluation
paper_authors: Aditya Mittal, Ryan Shar, Zichu Wu, Shyam Agarwal, Tongshuang Wu
